ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurosurgery Consultation — Mary Shelley

code.originalText: MRI and EEG results, start of levetiracetam, and neurosurgical consultation

text.paragraph: Headaches with recurrent episodes of numbness and weakness of the right hand and leg, one with twitching of the fingers and one with word-finding difficulty, and mild right-hand weakness, in a 51-year-old writer; urgent MRI with gadolinium and an EEG are booked this week. If they show a structural lesion, please see her to explain the options and plan treatment with her. [S]
Urgency: Urgent, within two weeks of the MRI. [S]

list.item: If the MRI shows a meningioma or other tumor, what are her options (observation, resection, or stereotactic radiosurgery), and which do you advise?
Should she start an antiseizure medicine now, and which one?
If there is swelling around a lesion, does she need dexamethasone, and if so for how long?
If surgery is chosen, what will the pathology add (WHO CNS5 grade), and what further treatment and imaging follow-up should we expect?
What should she be told about driving and about returning to writing?

text.paragraph: Ms. Shelley is seen at the request of Dr. Achterberg-Ilesanmi. She describes about two years of headaches, now most mornings, and over six months five brief spells beginning in the right fingers with tingling, sometimes twitching of the thumb, and weakness spreading toward the elbow and once into the leg, each lasting one to three minutes with full awareness; once she could not find words for a minute. The last was five days ago. She has dropped her pen during a spell, and her right hand tires when she writes. No vomiting, visual loss, or falls. She stopped driving two weeks ago. She asked to see every image and had read about meningioma before the visit. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London on August 30, 1797, the only child of the writer Mary Wollstonecraft and the philosopher William Godwin. [D]
Her mother died in London on September 10, 1797, eleven days after the birth, of puerperal fever; her father wrote that the placenta had been retained and had to be removed by hand. [D]
Her first child, a daughter born prematurely in February 1815, died after a few days. [D]
She began the tale that became Frankenstein in Switzerland in the summer of 1816, and Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus was published anonymously in January 1818, when she was 20. [D]
Her daughter Clara died in Italy in 1818, at about one year, and her son William died in Italy in June 1819, at three; she then had no living children. [D]
Her son Percy Florence, born in November 1819, was the only one of her four children to survive childhood. [D]
In June 1822 she nearly died of hemorrhage after a miscarriage about three months into a pregnancy; her husband stopped the bleeding by placing her in ice baths. [D]

In July 1822 her husband, the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, drowned while sailing in the Gulf of Spezia, leaving her a widow before she was 25, with a son of two; she decided to earn her living by her writing and by publishing his. [D]
She published the novels Valperga (1823) and The Last Man (1826), a revised Frankenstein (1831), and Rambles in Germany and Italy (1844). [D]

At about fourteen she had a very painful skin condition of one entire arm, treated with poultices; at times she could not move the arm and wore it in a sling. It has been interpreted as eczema, psoriasis, or chickenpox. [D]

In her journal in June 1840 she wrote that she had been long oppressed by care, disappointment, and ill health, and that lately ill health and extreme depression had marred what little she could do for others. [D]

From 1839 she had recurrent severe headaches of varying severity, site, and duration, with dizziness, pain in the legs, right hand, and right eye, brief episodes of partial paralysis of the right leg and hand, tremors, and convulsive seizures. Her physicians called the illness psychosomatic in 1842, a functional derangement of the nerves or brain in 1845, and neuralgia of the heart in 1846. [D]
From 1846 to 1851 she lived at 24 Chester Square, Belgravia, London, and spent time at Field Place in Sussex, the home of her son and his wife after their marriage in 1848. [D]

list.item: Left frontoparietal convexity meningioma with vasogenic edema (D32.0). The appearance is typical of a meningioma. Because it causes seizures and weakness and is surrounded by edema, observation is not appropriate. Stereotactic radiosurgery works best for small tumors without mass effect; at 3.1 cm with edema next to the motor cortex it carries a real risk of worsening the swelling, and it gives no tissue for grading. Surgical resection with its dural attachment (Simpson grade I) is the treatment of choice, is likely to be curative, and should relieve the seizures. The main risk is weakness of the right hand, usually temporary, which motor mapping during surgery reduces. She chose resection. [S]

Focal epilepsy due to the meningioma (G40.109). Recurrent focal aware seizures with a causative lesion and an epileptiform EEG: an antiseizure medicine is indicated now. Levetiracetam suits her, with few interactions; its main drawback is irritability or low mood, which should be watched given her history. [S]

Edema and corticosteroids. The deficit is mild and stable, so dexamethasone is not needed now. A short course from three days before surgery, tapered over about ten days afterwards, reduces brain swelling around the operation; longer use brings more harm than benefit. [S]

Pathology and follow-up. Grade decides adjuvant treatment. After complete resection of a CNS WHO grade 1 meningioma, radiation is not needed and follow-up is by MRI; grade 2 or 3 features (mitotic count, brain invasion, TERT promoter mutation, or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion) would lead to a discussion of radiation. [S]

Driving and writing. She should not drive until she has been seizure-free for the period her state requires and I have reviewed her after surgery. Writing can resume as soon as she feels able; occupational therapy helps if the hand is slow to recover. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: MRI of the brain with gadolinium eleven days ago: a 3.1 x 2.7 x 2.6 cm extra-axial, dural-based, uniformly enhancing mass on the left frontoparietal convexity over the hand area of the precentral gyrus, with a dural tail, a cerebrospinal fluid cleft, moderate vasogenic edema, and a 2 mm midline shift; no other lesion; MR angiography normal. EEG a week ago: left central sharp waves and slowing. Blood count, metabolic panel, ECG, and Dr. Achterberg-Ilesanmi's examination. [S]

list.item: Left frontoparietal craniotomy with neuronavigation and motor mapping in three weeks, aiming at Simpson grade I resection. [S]
Levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day from today, continued for at least a year after surgery, then an EEG and a shared decision about tapering. [S]
Dexamethasone 4 mg twice a day from three days before surgery, tapered and stopped over about ten days afterwards; no steroid now. [S]
Blood count and clotting tests before surgery; MRI within 48 hours after surgery. [S]
Pathology with WHO CNS5 grading, including TERT promoter and CDKN2A/B testing; no radiation if grade 1 and completely resected. [S]
MRI at three months after surgery, then yearly for five years, then every two years. [S]
No driving until seizure-free for the period her state requires and cleared after surgery; occupational therapy if hand weakness persists. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Achterberg-Ilesanmi the same day. Ms. Shelley saw her images and was given a written summary of the three options and of her choice. [S]
Follow-up: Neurosurgery will see her before surgery, on the ward, and after the three-month MRI. Primary care follows the seizures, mood, and recovery in between. [S]
